newsitem.title: USA: Treasury chief attacks balanced budget amendment.
newsitem.headline: Treasury chief attacks balanced budget amendment.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Friday saw agreement this year on a plan to get rid of government red ink, but said a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution was not the way to do it.
"Politically, historically and economically, the forces are in place to balance the budget," Rubin told the Senate Judiciary Committee. "We are not far apart. Now we need to get the job done."

Both Democratic President Bill Clinton and Republican lawmakers who control Congress are committed to balancing the budget by the year 2002. Many Republicans, however, believe that needs to be buttressed by a Constitutional amendment.
Clinton earlier this year seemed to signal that he was backing away from his opposition to such an amendement, but Rubin made clear that was not the case.

"A balanced budget amendment is a threat to our economic health, will expose our economy to unacceptable risks and should not be adopted," Rubin said. "It would seriously increase the risk of default on national debt."

By tying the government's hands, a Constitutional amendment could turn economic slowdowns into recession and recessions into depressions, he said. It could also prevent the government from quickly dealing with emergencies, such as natural disasters or militray threats.

Passage of a Constitutional amendment requires a two-thirds vote by both the House of Representatives and the Senate. It does not need presidential approval, but must ratified by three-quarters of the states.
The House approved a balanced budget amendment two years ago but the measure failed by one vote in the Senate. This year, prospects of passage look better in the Senate than in the House.
Judiciary Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch argued that a balanced budget amendment was needed to stop the relentless rise of the goverment debt, which has already surpassed $4 trillion.

To underscore his point, the Utah Republican used two props -- an electronic bulletin board counting off the rise in the debt as it occured and a big bag containing $13,000 in cash that was dumped in front of the committee.
"Every three seconds the debt increases by more than $13,000," he said. "That is real debt that we are strapping on the backs of our children and grandchildren. It simply has to stop."
Rubin argued that Washington has the political will to balance the budget without a Constitutional amendment and said Clinton will introduce a plan early next month to do just that by the year 2002.
He shied away from giving any details, although he made clear later to reporters that the plan would not contain the deep cut in the capital gains tax being sought by Republicans.
The administration plan, though, will include other tax cuts aimed at helping the middle class.
"I believe we will put in place balanced budget legislation this year," Rubin said.
